utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, can you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Case Number IT-01-47-T, The Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Appearances for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours, counsel, and everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Mathias Neuner, Daryl Mundis, and Andres Vatter, the case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Appearances for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of General Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, counsel, and Muriel Cauvin, legal assistant. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The other Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Kubura, Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and Nermin Mulalic, legal assistant. I believe that we have a problems with the transcript. I don't know whether the others are experiencing the same problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I have been told that there are problems with the transcript, but on the laptop, you should be able to follow it. The other Defence team, do you have the transcript on your computers?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we have transcript on our little computer. But I don't know whether the witness's computer is working. I don't know how the witness is going to follow it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. If the witness can follow English, but if he doesn't, how is that going to be of any use to him?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, he can follow the end of the transcript on the computer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. I have been told that it will appear in a couple of minutes. In the meantime, I'm going to give you two pieces of information. First one concerns the Plenary Sessions of Judges which was originally scheduled for Monday, the 6th of December. Yesterday, I learned that the date was changed, and the Plenary Session is going to take place on the 8th of December, which is a Wednesday, which means that on the 8th of December we are not going to be sitting. We are going to experience problems with the witnesses that have been scheduled. There are two ways to solve this. Either you move the witness for another date, or you have the witness wait on the 8th of December. I don't have any other solutions to that problem. What do you think?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, since we have already asked for the visa to be obtained for the witness for the scheduled date, I believe that it would be best if the witness starts on the 6th, we make a break on the 8th, and we finish with this witness as per our original schedule. Mr. President, we are going to propose the time that we and the other participants might need for the examination-in-chief and the cross-examination in order to be as efficient as possible in the time that you have allocated for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The Prosecution, do you have anything to say about this date, the 8th of December, when we are not going to be sitting and the possible break that we can make in the testimony of this witness? This is a Defence witness, but just for the courtesy, could you please share with us your observations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We really take no position with respect to when the witness arrives or any breaks that might be necessary due to the plenary or any other reason. We simply once again reiterate that we will need for purposes of cross-examination the same amount of time that the Defence for Mr. Hadzihasanovic takes in their direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. The other issue that I would like to raise is the issue of documents which were -- which are contained in this binder. Could Mr. Registrar give us the numbers for these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. You have indicated the numbers, and I thank you for that. And we have completed this part of the session. We're going to bring the witness into the courtroom. Mr. Usher, can you please bring the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir. First of Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond all, I would like to make sure that you can hear my words in your language. If that is the case, can you please say, "I understand you and I hear you."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I hear you and understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have been called as a Defence witness. Before you make the solemn declaration, I would like to hear your name, your last name, your date of birth, and the place where you were born.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Samir Sefer is my name. I was born on the 1st of April, 1966 in Goles, Travnik Municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Sefer. Do you work? What is your profession at the moment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Currently, I am a private caterer. I am the owner of two catering establishments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. In 1992 and 1993, did you work? What was your profession? If you were a soldier, which unit did you belong to and what rank did you have at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1992, before the beginning of war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, I was also a private restaurant owner, and I had the same two catering establishments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And in 1993, did you also have these restaurants? Were you also a caterer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. When the war broke out in Bosnia and Herzegovina, at the very beginning I was a member of the village guards which belonged to the Territorial Defence of Travnik. And my attachment was called Karaula. It bore the same name as the place where I resided at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And at that moment, were you a member of an army unit or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I became a member of the army unit in the spring of 1993. I became a member of the commission attached to the operations group Bosanska Krajina. This was the commission which looked after the prisoners of war and the bodies of the dead soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: Very well. Have you ever testified before an international court or a national court regarding the things that happened in Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1992 and 1993? Or is this the first time ever that you testified in a court of law?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is the first time I have testified in an international court or the national courts in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Would you please read the solemn declaration the usher will give you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, you may be seated. Mr. Sefer, you have to testify. First you will answer questions put to you by the Defence teams. I'm sure that you have already met with them. They're seated on your left. After that, you are going to answer questions put to you by the representatives of the Prosecution seated to your right. The representatives of the Prosecution will have the same time as the Defence, which means an hour to an hour and a half. After this second stage of your testimony, the Defence teams will be given the opportunity to ask you supplementary questions arising from the questions of the Prosecution. The three Judges seated in front of you may also put questions to you. The Judges prefer to wait until both sides complete their respective examinations. You will maybe see that the two sets of questions differ in their nature. Try to answer as precisely as possible. If you don't know the answer, say so. If the answer seems too complicated, you may always ask the person who has put it to you to rephrase it. And you have to know that we don't have any written documents, and we very much rely on your testimony for the clarification of the events. I have to explain two other issues to you which are very important: First of all, you have taken the solemn declaration to tell the truth, which means you are not going to give us false testimony because this would be a violation of the law and you may be punished for that. And the second issue that I would like to inform you about is that if at any point in time you believe that an answer to any of the questions might incriminate you and be used against you, you may refuse to answer such a question. At that moment, the Chamber may compel you to answer such a question, but they will also guarantee you a sort of immunity. In very general terms, this is how your testimony is going to develop. After an hour and a half, we're going to take a break, which is going to give you an opportunity to take a rest because sometimes it may be tiring to answer all these questions. We will then resume around 11.00. Around half past 12.00, we are going to have another technical break. And in theory, if everything goes well, this hearing should be over around quarter to 2.00, and you will be allowed to return home. I'm now going to give the floor to the Defence teams.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Examined by Ms. Residovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Sefer.

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to the words of the President which you have just heard, I would like to draw your attention to another thing. The two of us speak the same language, and I'm sure that you will be in a position to answer my questions immediately. However, my questions and your answers have to be interpreted for the Trial Chamber and for everybody in the courtroom. That is why I would kindly ask you to make a little pause between my question and your answer. This will allow the interpreters to interpret your words correctly. Did you understand that?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've told us, Mr. Sefer, what you did before the war and what you are doing at the moment. What is your educational background and where did you acquire your education?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: I completed primary school in my native place, in Karaula, where I resided. I completed secondary school, and I graduated as a traffic technician in Travnik. After that, I went to serve in the army, in the JNA. And after the compulsory military service, I enrolled in the school of traffic at the University of Sarajevo. I stayed there for two years. Then I dropped out, and I started running the catering business that I've mentioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've just told us that you served in the JNA. Can you please tell me, in which branch of the army did you serve and did you acquire a rank?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: I served in Bela Crkva and in Sabac. I did not have a rank, and I was a car unit. I was a driver, in other words.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've also told us that you became a member of the Bosanska Krajina operations group. After that duty -- or let me first ask you, up to when did you stay in that position? And after that, did you have any other duties in the BiH Army? And thirdly, did you acquire a rank in the BiH Army?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to apologise and say that in addition to what I have said, I was also a member of the Territorial Defence. I stood guard in my village at the very beginning of the war. Immediately after the beginning of war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, I was first a member of the state commission for exchange, and then sometime in spring 1993 when the Bosanska Krajina operations group was established pursuant to an order of the general staff of the BiH Army for the establishment of commissions for prisoners of war and bodies of the fallen soldiers, this was in April or May 1993, and I was appointed the president of that commission affiliated with the operations group. I stayed in that position sometime up to November 1993. And then I moved to Zenica, and I Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond became the president of the commission for prisoners of war affiliated with the 3rd Corps. I remained in that position up to the establishment of the 7th Corps. And then I returned to my own place, to Travnik, which was the headquarters of that corps. And that is where I became the president of the commission in charge of the prisoners of war affiliated with the 7th Corps. You've also asked me about my rank. During the war, I did not have a rank. And once the Dayton Accords were signed and the war was over, during the last stages of the war, I was given the rank of second lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much for this very elaborate answer. Let me go back to the beginning of your answer. You said that in 1992, you became a member of the municipal commission for exchange. Could you please tell us how you became a member of that commission, who appointed you as a member of that commission.

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: As I've already said at the beginning, after the beginning of war, we started standing guard in the village, and we were members of the Travnik Territorial Defence. At the same time as we were standing guard during the night, during the day, I would stay in my restaurant in Travnik. It was a fast food restaurant. Very often, I had police officers, Mr. Beba Salko, and Enez Hadzimovic. I knew that they worked in the police and the police building was very close. I got rather close with them --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would just like to interrupt for a moment. Maybe this is a bit too wide. You've mentioned Mr. Salko Beba. Did he have any connection with the exchange commission and your engagement in that commission?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Beba Salko was the president of the municipal state commission for exchanges, and he appointed me as a member of that commission.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sefer, do you remember the first task you had when involved in these exchanges?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: First task -- first duties I had to perform were those of a lorry driver. Exchanges of dead MUP members and of television employees, the employees of the BH TV had to be exchanged. These were workers who secured the relay on Vlasic. They had been killed by the JNA. And I went to collect the bodies of these men who had been killed. I went there as a lorry driver.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the president of that state commission for exchanges in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: As far as I remember, when the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina issued the order to establish such a state commission for exchanges, I think that Esad Muhibic was the first president. And shortly afterwards, Amor Masovic replaced him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember who the president was and who the members of your municipal commission were?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: Well, I just said the president of the municipal commission was Mr. Beba Salko. In addition to myself, Mr. Jasenko Eminovic was a member of the commission, he was a reserve police officer. And then there was Dr. Sakib Alibegovic, a psychiatrist. Then there was Bajo Zvonko, and Tomo Rajic who represented the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sefer, I want to continue to ask you questions about 1992. Tell me: How did you perform those duties, and how much work did the commission during that period?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: Well, Beba Salko was the key figure as the president. And we carried out the following tasks together with him: We were involved in exchange of prisoners and the bodies of those who had been killed, and we also had to receive refugees who had arrived from Bosanska Krajina in Travnik during that period.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you go back to that period up until the time you joined the Bosanska Krajina operations group, could you tell us how many refugees arrived in the Travnik area?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: At the time, there were a lot of refugees arriving from Bosanska Krajina. And soon, Jajce fell as well as my place, Karaula. So during that period, we received between one hundred and fifty and two hundred thousand refugees.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any tasks in the commission with regard to these refugees and these people who had been expelled?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: Well, I was involved in receiving those refugees. Eminovic Jasenko worked with me. But as the number of these refugees grew, Jasenko would sometimes be involved in other activities. Or rather, he would remain in the office where he took various statements and interviewed people together with Dr. Salko. And I and other members would go into the field, go to the places where these people had been left by the Serbian aggressor, and these people were then sent off towards Travnik or towards the free territory by the Serbian aggressor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, was movement difficult for those refugees and for members of the commission? What sort of work did you have to do? What sort of problems did you have to confront?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: Well, this is when I first felt that we were really in a state of war because at the very beginning when the war had just broken out, it seemed to be a game. However, when I saw all these people arriving, these people who had suffered so much, people who were wandering aimlessly who didn't know which routes to take because they had been abandoned in the evening at about 2300 or 2400 hours, well, we would come across old people who had been sitting there for three or four days and were unable to continue their journey. So it was a traumatic experience for me, and I am still under the impression of this experience to this very day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In addition to the duties you performed in the state commission, before you joined the Bosanska Krajina operations group, did you become involved in any other duties? Did you carry out any other tasks for Mr. Beba in your capacity as a member of the commission?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: In addition to my active participation in the municipal commission, I was actively involved in all the negotiations conducted by Mr. Beba with the Serbian and Montenegrin aggressor. My role in those negotiations was to guard the vehicles, to talk to Serbian soldiers, to survey the surroundings. After exchanges, I would speak to Mr. Beba and provide him with the information I had obtained while spending time up there. This was interesting for him. So after each exchange, I had to draft an official report for him in which I was to tell him whether I had observed anything that might be of interest to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As part of the exchange of prisoners and when receiving these people, these refugees, when involved in these tasks, did you cooperate with any international institutions or forces in order to carry out the exchanges as well as possible?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: Well, what did these negotiations look like? At the very beginning, we would cross over to the Serbian side and go deep into their territory. We always insisted on UNPROFOR presence. We always insisted on the International Red Cross being present. However, usually, they would not allow them to cross over into their territory. So usually, we crossed over into their territory on our own.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the course of the exchanges themselves, would these exchanges take place at the time of combat operations, or did any international organisations assume the responsibility of arranging a cease-fire?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: Well, this was one of the reasons for which we insisted on UNPROFOR teams or Red Cross teams being present whenever we were involved in negotiations because they could provide a guarantee for obtaining a cease-fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In response to a question put to you by the Presiding Judge, you said that in spring, in April or in May, you became the president of the commission in the operations group Bosanska Krajina. Tell me, what sort of tasks did that commission have?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: Yes, I can't remember when it was exactly. It was in the spring, April or May 1993. That was when I was appointed as president of the commission for prisoners of war and for men who had been killed. We were involved in taking care of prisoners of war and taking care of members of Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond the BH Army who had been killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time, was it your duty to establish contact with the Serbian forces, or were there requests for negotiations with the forces who were becoming Bosnia and Herzegovina's new enemy?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: Well, yes, I still maintained regular contact with the Serbian and Montenegrin aggressor. And during that period, when these events were unfolding in the Lasva Valley, on the Serbian side, there was an UNHCR convoy, and there was an International Red Cross convoy that appeared. And I was involved in taking charge of the convoy arriving from the Serbian territory. I had to escort the convoy through our territory, and then return the convoy to Serbian territory. As the conflict continued, it became necessary to establish contact with HVO representatives because we were being told that our combatants were being imprisoned and that the bodies of our men would remain in their territory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were the premises of your municipal commission for exchange?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: The premises were in an office near Travnik Municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you assumed your new duties, in which part of Travnik did you continue to work?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: As the new president for the commission of prisoners of war in the Bosanska Krajina operations group, my office remained in the same place, in the same premises used by the municipal commission. And we continued to cooperate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sefer, you have just answered my next question. Was there close cooperation with the municipal state commission when you performed your tasks?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: Yes. We cooperated very closely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, at the time, were your tasks divided when communicating with certain parts of the other armies that you had to cooperate with?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: I apologise. I didn't quite understand that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to know whether you were involved in all forms of communication with the Serbian Army and the HVO or were there -- was there certain division of work? Were some people involved in certain tasks and others in other tasks?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: Well, we worked together. During the initial period we hadn't yet established contact with the HVO commission so we acted together in negotiations with the Serbian and Montenegrin aggressor. It wasn't a matter of prestige. We were pursuing our own interests. But on the whole, I was more often than not interested in the combatants of the BH Army alone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sefer, since you have mentioned some names already, tell me whether at any point in time in 1993, Beba Salko assumed other duties? And in particular, I would like to know whether he assumed any duties in the Bosanska Krajina operations group?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: Well, I'll try to go back to that period. It could have been in June. That was when Beba Salko was appointed as the assistant commander for security in the Bosanska Krajina operations group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know which tasks the member of the state commission, Jasenko was involved in during that period of time?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: Well, Jasenko Eminovic continued to work in the municipal commission as a member of the reserve police force in Travnik. He remained a member. Sometimes he went to help Salko. This involved computer work, drafting documents, et cetera. But on the whole, he was with me in the commission for exchanges.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Sefer, in addition to the duties you had when involved in exchanges, were you assigned duties that involved providing security, for example, related to BH Army members?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: Yes. During the first few days of the conflict with the HVO, I interviewed BH Army members who had committed offences of various kinds. I was involved in other cases, too, and I would take statements from these men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sefer, on the whole, can you tell me about the kind of offences the BH Army members committed most frequently?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: Well, usually they refused to obey orders. There were -- there was looting. They would break into abandoned houses, flats. So those are the sort of things they did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sefer, for how long were you involved in these matters?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: Well, very briefly, because I found this work very difficult, especially because I knew all these men. These men simply couldn't understand that an army could prosecute them for stealing Croatian property, et cetera. So it was hard for me to walk around the town. I was quite simply afraid. I was in a difficult position, and I could hardly wait to abandon those duties and quickly requested -- I soon requested Mr. Beba to relieve of those duties which he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During that brief period of time when you were involved in investigating combatants, do you remember how many combatants were the subject of such investigations?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly. But there were scores of them. Every day, I would take over 10 statements. And there are many such cases but I cannot remember the exact number because I never went to the prison. I didn't see them there. I simply had to take statements from these men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You just mentioned the prison. Were these army members detained? Were disciplinary measures taken against them? Were prosecutions instituted?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's now move on to another subject, because I think you have answered all the questions that I wanted to put to you. A minute ago, you said that you had no contact with the HVO commission. Nevertheless, in June, as the president of the commission for prisoners of war for the BH Army, did you find out about a large-scale exchange, or does the name humanitarian commission mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar with that case. It involved an exchange arranged by the humanitarian commission. I don't know who the members of the commission were. I know that the order was that all prisoners and civilians should be released. All of those prisoners and civilians who wanted to move over to the Croatian side. I was present during the exchange when we let the civilians and prisoners that we had move over to the Croatian side. I also heard that all the prisoners who were in the KP Dom in Zenica, the penal and correctional facility in Zenica were released. However, experience subsequently demonstrated that many of our combatants who were in prisons with the HVO had been hidden, and they weren't released. So I had many difficulties as a result when carrying out my duties, since I didn't have any prisoners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sefer, tell me, were you issued an order stating where these prisoners should be sent, the prisoners who might have been captured in the course of combat by the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: Yes. The order was that as soon as they were imprisoned, all prisoners should be sent to the Zenica KP Dom, penal and correctional facility.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if there were criminal proceedings instituted against any of the prisoners? And if so, what would happen to these prisoners?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: Yes. Some prisoners were prosecuted. I know that they were released and that the municipal court in Travnik would assume responsibility for them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sefer, tell me, when you as the president of the commission of the operations group first established contact with the HVO, tell me, when did you first establish contact in that capacity in the HVO and how did you do it?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: In spite of the pressure I exerted on the International Red Cross and UNPROFOR and in spite of my request for them to organise a meeting with representatives from the Croatian side, such a meeting never materialised. Quite by chance, I found out through a radio -- that a radiolink was established with Vitez, between Travnik and Vitez. I went to that place and I contacted the person who worked on that radio set in Vitez, and I asked him to provide me or find me an HVO member who could Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond talk to me about exchanges of prisoners of war and about exchanges of the bodies of killed men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember when this happened? When did you first have contact with the other side with regard to such exchanges?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: Well, the exact period, I can't really remember the exact period. Perhaps it was in August or September. I'm really not sure though. However, I do know that the first time I established contact, it was with Zarko Andric, also known as Zuti. He was looking for a relative of his -- rather, he was looking for his brother's son. He was looking for his body which had remained somewhere in the area of Velika Bukovica. All he was interested in was finding that body. And when we first spoke to each other, he offered me money for me to hand over that body to him. I refused to cooperate in this way. I told him that he would be given the body if I found it, and I said that there would be no conditions. However, I said that if I did this, I also wanted an exchange of men who were still alive, prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sefer, after you had established initial contact, did you exchange the body of Mr. Andric's relative, and after doing that, was there any cooperation or attempted cooperation with the commission for exchanges on the HVO side?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: Well, after we had come to this arrangement, after I'd come to this arrangement with Mr. Zuti, I went into the field. I managed to find Andric Dominko's body, and I arranged for an exchange with Zuti. However, a difficult situation arose. Mr. Zuti didn't want to go to the area between the lines. He wanted me to go down. I didn't want to. We managed to reach an agreement according to which the prisoners I were requesting would be placed in a van by him. He would get someone to drive the van to our territory, and I was then to send his dead relative and the other prisoners whom I had included in the exchange of HVO prisoners. This is how the first exchange took place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sefer, tell me whether you later met with the commission, and did you start holding meetings in order to attempt to obtain exchanges of prisoners or dead BH Army members held by the HVO and dead HVO members held by the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: After those first talks, I used the same radiolink to talk to Zarko Andric, aka Zuti. We arranged another exchange of men who had been killed. However, since this concerned men who had been killed, we weren't able to carry out the exchange in the same manner that we had carried the first exchange out. We had to find another means. We agreed that I should move over into their territory and to carry out the exchange. I informed the International Red Cross and UNPROFOR about our agreement and about the day on which we would carry out this exchange, and I asked them to be present during the exchange because this was to be the first time I was going to cross over to HVO territory. However, just before the exchange, the International Red Cross and UNPROFOR promised to attend the exchange. However, just before the exchange, perhaps an hour before the exchange, they informed me that they couldn't attend the exchange. They said that the HVO wouldn't allow it. And since my safety wasn't guaranteed, they said I should abandon this attempt. However, at the time I was really determined to carry out the exchange, so I got hold of a lorry, put the dead bodies into the lorry and went deep into HVO territory. Perhaps 10 kilometres into HVO territory. And that's the first time I met Zuti. And in a cafe at Kajic's, he said that HVO representatives were waiting for me. He said, "This isn't a job for me, I don't like to do this, but there are people who will negotiate with you." And when I entered that cafe, that was the first time I met individual members of the HVO commission with whom I continued to cooperate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sefer, tell me, you've told me how you established contact with the HVO. But who did you rely on and who did you cooperate in subordinate units in order to obtain information on the identity of prisoners and fallen soldiers?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: Well, in the corps, the department for morale was concerned with prisoners of war and killed army members. And assistant commanders for morale, the people with whom I established contact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Once you established contact with the HVO commission in autumn 1993, did you manage to carry out any other exchanges with the HVO?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: My first contact with the HVO commission was not successful. All of my requests, all of my demands were denied by the HVO commission. They said they didn't know these men, and whatever name I mentioned, they said they didn't have a clue who that was. And that first meeting showed me and explained to me why representatives of the international organisations did not want to be present at that meeting. When I returned from that meeting, as I was getting into the car, Zuti approached me, said good-bye to me. And as he was saying his good-byes, he said on Kaonik there are seven prisoners of war from your side, and the others that you're looking for, they were killed in the cinema hall in Vitez. And the HVO are in possession of the photos of their dead bodies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After that, were there exchanges in spite of all that? What problems did you encounter when you were looking for prisoners of war? Were you aware of the fact that members of the BH Army were killed once they were taken prisoner?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: After my first meeting with the HVO commission, the International Red Cross and UNPROFOR provided for another meeting in the UNPROFOR base in Bila, in Vitez. At that meeting, we managed to agree on a small-scale exchange. However, our relationship soon deteriorated because the HVO had captured four of our members from Preocica and Vitez. And that same night, it showed them on TV as being interviewed. However, in my next contact with the HVO commission, they told me that those men had never been captured alive, that they had been killed in combat. Later on, I managed to obtain their bodies during an exchange. Representatives of the International Red Cross and European Monitors were present during that exchange. We took photos of those dead bodies which were completely massacred and mutilated. And how shall I put it? When the exchange was taking place, a policeman who was providing security and who was a member of the HVO put something in my pocket and told me, "don't look at it now. Look at it when you return to your base." When I left their territory, as I left no-man's-land and I arrived at our territory, I opened that piece of paper, and there was an eye wrapped in that piece of paper. I showed it to the European Monitors. Later on, I learned that a message was heard on the radio: "This is Hurim's eye. We're not bad people. We didn't want to keep the eye of the dead man."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sefer, in autumn 1993, did you ever learn that several people, several prominent Croats had been taken away from Travnik? If you ever learned, that who did you learn that from and how?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: I learned about this incident. It was a terrible incident that shook the entire city because the people who were taken away were very popular and very well-known in the town. The first time I learned about that case was from Mrs. Ljilja Popovic who came to the commission in order to report the disappearance of her husband.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mrs. Popovic talk to you and what did you do on the following day? What did you hear on the following day? First of all, can you remember when this took place?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: I believe that this was some time in October, mid-October, towards the end of October 1993. When she came to the commission, she didn't talk to me personally. We referred her to Mr. Beba Salko because he was in charge of civilians. That's why we sent her to his office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During those days, did you find out who had taken these people away? What measures were taken within the operations group?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: I don't know exactly when, but very soon there were rumours in town that this had been done by the Mujahedin. However, I never knew exactly what had happened. I know that Mr. Beba was particularly engaged in solving this case, and I know that the command asked me to do something about it because later on it was heard that some Mujahedins had allegedly Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond been captured by the HVO, and that's why the Mujahedin had captured Croats, because they wanted to exchange those Croats for the people who had allegedly been captured by the HVO. The pressure put on us by the commanders and the civilians was huge. That's why we tried to solve this case. I tried to establish contact with the HVO commission to find out what had happened and to see whether indeed Mujahedin had been captured. The answer that I received from the HVO was that they did not have any such people, any such dead bodies. So I was not in a position to help resolve that case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was it who continued dealing with this issue? Who persisted in the attempt to liberate these people from the Mujahedins' hands?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: It was Mr. Beba Salko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any international factors in Travnik get engaged and involved? Did they try to put pressure on the HVO and the mujahedin in order to have these people from Travnik released?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: Yes. It was the International Red Cross who got involved. There was a young woman whose name I believe was Mary. I can't remember her last name. I know that she stayed in Zenica, and she was in charge of Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever learn what happened to these people, to these Croats who had been taken away from Travnik? Were they ever set free, and when did you learn that?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: During that period of time, from the moment they were taken away from Travnik I was appointed the president of the commission with the 3rd Corps. This was in November 1993. That's when I left for Zenica. Later on, maybe in January or in February of the following year, I learned that these people had been released.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were in Travnik and while you were following those efforts and in a certain way participated in the efforts to have your neighbours set free, did you know at the time whether these people were alive or maybe did you have any information that something might have happened to them?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: No, I didn't have any such information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sefer, I'm going to ask you as follows: In 1993, from the moment you became the president of the commission affiliated with the operations group until the moment of your departure in November, did you ever exchange a foreigner, especially an Arab or a Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: No, no, I didn't. Never. I can't remember whether there were any dead bodies of that sort. However, those dead bodies that were exchanged were very -- had been dead for a long time. It was very difficult to recognise their facial features. But I don't remember ever having exchanged a foreigner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sefer, in June, did you go to Guca Gora? If that was the case, who did you go with and why?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: As I've already explained, I was involved in taking statements from the BH Army members. And most of that took place in the office of the commission for exchanges. On one occasion during that period of time when I visited Guca Gora, Mr. Beba arrived and told me and Jasenko: "It seems that the monastery in Guca Gora had been set on fire. Let's go and see whether this information is correct." We heard it on the Serbian radio. Since the access to Guca Gora was very difficult because this part of the road was being shelled by the HVO, he told me, "Cento - this was my nickname - Cento, you drive. You're the best driver. Let's get into the Golf and let's go and see what had happened." This is when we went to Guca Gora.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived up there what did you see? Had the monastery been set on fire?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: No. We only noticed the military police, members of the local brigade which was the 306th Brigade, which provided security for the monastery. We parked in front of the monastery. We entered the monastery, and we saw that there were things scattered all over the monastery. You could see bulletholes on the walls, and you could see some Arabic inscriptions on the walls as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any other persons save for the military policemen? Did you see any priests, journalists, or anybody else?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: As far as I remember, there was somebody there. I don't know whether he stayed there. But he was there. He was a priest. And there were some journalists. I did not get any closer. I stayed at the very entrance to the monastery on the doorstep. And Mr. Beba spoke with this priest who he found there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sefer, did you do something when you saw the state of disarray in the monastery and the inscriptions on the walls?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: Yes. After the conversation that Mr. Beba had with the priest and the people who were standing there, he approached me and Jasenko and he said, "There is some white paint in the Golf. These paint over these inscriptions." I went back to the car. I took this paint. This paint was there because maybe a day or two days before, we had painted the walls of our office at the commission. We drew the image of a white UNPROFOR jeep, and we did it so that people could recognise us. That's why I had the paint. I took it from the car. I brought it to the monastery, and we painted over all of these inscriptions that we found in the monastery.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did members of the 306th Brigade tell you who had damaged the monastery and who had put those inscriptions on the walls?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: No, they didn't tell me personally. Later on, I heard in my conversation with Beba while travelling back in the car that this had been done by the Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Bearing in mind your job and what you did at the time, did you continue dealing with this issue? Did you go back to Guca Gora?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: No, I didn't go back to Guca Gora. This was the only time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. This completes my examination-in-chief of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like to ask the other Defence team if they have any questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President. We don't have any questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is quarter past 10.00. Maybe it would be a good thing to make a break now, or if the Prosecution should wish to start, we can start now. What do you want to do? Make a break or start now?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I would propose that we do, in fact, take the break, and that way I can streamline the cross-examination and ensure that there's enough time for the Chamber to ask any questions that they may have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are going to take a break. It is quarter past 10.00. We shall resume at quarter to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Cross-examined by Mr. Mundis:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. My name is Daryl Mundis, and along with my colleagues here today, we represent the Prosecution in this case. I have some questions for you this morning, and I just want to ensure at the outset that you understand that my purpose here is not to confuse you in any way. And as a result, if there are any questions that you don't understand, I would ask you, please, just to tell me that, and I will either clarify the question or rephrase the question so that you do understand.

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you mentioned this morning in response to a question from my learned colleague from the Defence that at some point in June 1993, Mr. Beba was appointed assistant commander for security of the operation group Bosanska Krajina. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To the best of your recollection, did Mr. Beba hold any other position with operation group Bosanska Krajina prior to June 1993, leaving aside, of course, the commission?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: I don't remember. Up to the moment he was appointed the assistant commander for security in the operations group, the only job he had was in the municipal commission for exchanges, and I also know that he was a policeman. But that's all I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let me, then, turn to your role during the period in June 1993. I take it from your answers earlier with respect to your involvement in some investigations that you, in fact, followed Mr. Beba to the security department of the operations group Bosanska Krajina in June 1993. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: No, no, it wouldn't. My only job was in the commission for the exchanges of prisoners of war. I said that only from time to time on a couple of occasions only I went to help take statements from those members of the BiH Army for whom it was suspected that they had committed some sort of a crime or offence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just so we're clear, then, sir, at no point in June 1993 were you affiliated with the security department of the operations group Bosanska Krajina?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: No, no, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You weren't a security officer in OG Bosanska Krajina in June 1993?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: I was not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you, you said that on occasion, you were asked to help take statements from those members of the BiH Army for whom it was suspected that they had committed some sort of a crime or offence. Do you recall the first time you were asked to assist in this respect? Approximately what time period or date?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: I can't remember the exact date. I remember that it was at the very beginning of the conflict with the HVO. As soon as Mr. Beba was appointed the assistant commander for security in the OG, myself and Jasenko started helping him. However, Jasenko was the one who helped him more often. I helped him only on a couple of occasions. There were quite a huge number of BiH Army members who were taken into custody and statements had to be taken from them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said it was shortly after Mr. Beba was appointed assistant commander. Do you recall the date that that appointment took place?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: Like I've already said, I can't remember the exact date, but I believe that it was in June 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you recall -- you said you assisted him only on a couple of occasions. Do you recall the last time that you assisted him with respect to taking statements from ABiH soldiers suspected of committing offences?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: This assistance could not have lasted more than a week or ten days. Due to a large influx of refugees from Bosanska Krajina, I had to drop that and I had to go back to my old job and look after all of these refugees from Bosanska Krajina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So I take it, then, sir, that these couple of occasions where you assisted Mr. Beba in this respect was sometime during the month of June 1993? And that's about all you can recall at this point about the time period?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, do you recall approximately how many ABiH soldiers who were suspected of committing crimes you spoke to during this period in June 1993?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: A huge number. Every day, I would take anything between five and ten statements. And this lasted throughout the entire week while I was there assisting Mr. Beba.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So you're telling us now that you spent an entire week taking statements from these ABiH soldiers who were suspected of committing crimes?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: It wouldn't take a whole day, but every day I would go there to take statements because ABiH Army members were being taken into constant custody, all the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, if you took between five and ten statements over a one-week period, can you estimate how many statements you might have taken from these soldiers?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: Maybe 30 or so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also said in response to questions earlier this morning that you - and this is at page 18, line 22 - you said "I knew these men." Do you recall the names of any of the soldiers suspected of committing crimes that you interviewed during the month of June 1993?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps I can remember a couple of names. Perhaps I can't remember the exact names. I know someone called Face. His real name was Fatmir Smajlovic. I know Goran Mevludin, aka Mevko. Mostly, these were familiar individuals, but I can't exactly remember the names of the men concerned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you also told us or you gave us two examples of the types of offences that you were questioning individuals about during the month of June 1993. You mentioned on page 18, about line 11, looting and refusal to obey orders.

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember any other offences for which you questioned ABiH soldiers during the month of June 1993?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: Well, since I mentioned these two individuals whom I remember, because I knew them well before the war, for example, Fatmir Smajlovic, Face, entered an abandoned Croatian flat. I don't know whether you're aware of this, but in part of the town of Travnik, most of the Croatian population, in agreement with the Serbian and Montenegrin aggressor, moved over to the Serbian side when the conflict with the HVO broke out. And a lot of their flats were abandoned. And in all these cases when I took statements from these men, the offences were related to breaking into these flats without authorisation, and the offences also involved the looting of these flats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these flats -- these looting incidents that you're telling us about all concerned property in the town of Travnik. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: In the town of Travnik and its surroundings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give me some examples of looting incidents from the surrounding area of Travnik that you questioned ABiH soldiers about during June 1993?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: I can't exactly remember the number of such cases there were. But I know that houses in Ovcarevo and Paklarevo were broken into. These were villages where the Croatian population was in the majority. And they had left these villages and crossed over to the Serbian side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Other than these incidents that you've told us about just now, do you recall any other incidents where you interviewed ABiH soldiers suspected of committing any other offence?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: As I said, when I took statements from these men, and the statements mostly concerned the looting of abandoned flats and houses and breaking into those abandoned flats and houses without the authorisation of the proper authorities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, I believe you told us earlier that when you were with the municipal commission, that your office was in Travnik, and I believe you said during or near the municipal building in Travnik. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the time -- can you tell us approximately the time frame or the range of approximate dates when you worked out of that office.

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: I started working in that office in June 1992 as a member of the municipal commission for exchanges. I remained there until I was appointed as the president of the commission for prisoners of war and for men who had been killed within the 3rd Corps. This was around November in 1993. That's when I moved to the corps command in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the period from November 1992 until November 1993, were you aware of which units of the 3rd Corps of the ABiH were stationed in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: No. Because I didn't know much about these military matters. I had information on our local brigades from Travnik, but I didn't know much about these other matters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "our local brigades from Travnik" can you tell us what you mean by that? What were the local brigades from Travnik?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: Well, I know for sure that in Travnik, there was the 312th Motorised Brigade because in that area we would move towards the Serbian and Montenegrin aggressor, and these men were from the 312th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Any other brigades from Travnik?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: All I know is that occasionally, the 17th Krajina Brigade was present in the area. I don't know whether they had their command there or not, but they were present in the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you know if there was a battalion of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade in Travnik during that time period?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know, sir, what unit or units of the ABiH 3rd Corps were in the former JNA barracks in Travnik during this time period?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you a few questions, sir, about your work with the municipal exchange commission. As part of your responsibilities with that commission, was it your job to be familiar with which soldiers were being detained by the ABiH and at what locations so that you could facilitate the exchange of these prisoners?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: During the period you mentioned, I was only a member of the municipal commission for exchanges. As far as the negotiations and discussions with the other side are concerned and as far as the prisoners we had, well, Mr. Beba was familiar with these matters. At the time, I was just a driver and an assistant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Just so that we're clear, then, sir, part of your responsibilities -- or your responsibilities did not include having or accumulating information as to the identities, number of detained HVO soldiers, and the locations of these detained HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: It was -- I only became involved in these matters when I became responsible for the commission for taking care of prisoners of war within the Bosanska Krajina operations group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's talk about that period of time, then, sir. That was -- can you refresh our recollection as to the approximate date when you assumed that responsibility.

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: I assumed those responsibility in April or May 1993. I don't know the exact date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And from April or May 1993 until the time when you began working for the 3rd Corps commission on exchange, did your responsibilities include accumulating information about detained soldiers of the HVO, their names, and where they were being held by various units of the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: I did have to know which Croatian prisoners we had in order to be able to negotiate with the HVO and in order to be able to ask them for BiH Army prisoners. Since I had received such orders, I knew that all Croatian prisoners weren't being kept in units. It was through the department for morale in the corps that I obtained lists of imprisoned Croats who were soon transferred to the Zenica KP Dom after they had been captured.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you a follow-on questions. You told us it was the corps department of morale that provided you with the list of imprisoned Croats?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: Yes. I've already mentioned the structure of the commission. I said that assistant commanders for morale in brigades were with me, and there was the department for morale within the corps. And I established contact in the corps through Mrs. Emira Bolic who was also president at the time for the commission of prisoners of war in the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, at what point in time did you begin receiving information from the morale department of the corps concerning detained HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: Well, I was always receiving information. When a Croatian soldier was captured, I would be informed that he was being detained. At the same time, I received requests according to which I was to find out where captured members of the BH Army were held.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this would date back from the time period when in April and May of 1993 when you were responsible for the exchange commission of the OG Bosanska Krajina? At that point in time, you were already receiving information from the corps?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: Yes. From the time I was appointed as president of the commission in the Bosanska Krajina operations group, from that time onwards, I was in contact with the president for the commission for prisoners of war in the 3rd Corps, Mrs. Emira Bolic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you also mentioned the assistant commander for morale. Did that individual play a role in providing you with this information as to detained HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: On the whole, these assistant commanders in units provided me with information on captured members of the BiH Army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I'm sorry, sir. When I mentioned the assistant commander for morale, I meant the 3rd Corps assistant commander for morale. Was that individual providing you with information on detained HVO soldiers who were being held by ABiH 3rd Corps units from the period April-May 1993 onwards?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: The assistant commander for morale in the 3rd Corps did not provide information to me. He provides such information to my boss because Mrs. Emira Bolic was my superior. I was president of the commission for POWs in the operations group. And Emira Bolic was responsible for the commission within the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the information that the 3rd Corps assistant commander for morale received, do you know where he got that from? Did he get that from the brigades or battalions that were actually holding the HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: I don't know how he obtained that information. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've also told us on several occasions this morning that the detained HVO soldiers were to be kept at the Zenica KP Dom. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware at any point in time in 1993 whether there were detained HVO soldiers being held in locations other than KP Dom Zenica?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: No I wasn't aware of it. I knew that in my zone of responsibility, that is to say, in the Bosanska Krajina OG zone of responsibility, I knew that soldiers from the units were taken to the barracks and soon afterwards they were transferred to the Zenica KP Dom. And these are the orders that we received.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And sir, when you say "soldiers from the units were taken to the barracks," first of all, can you tell me what you mean by barracks?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: I don't know how much you know about this, but there is a barracks in Travnik which is where the command of the Bosanska Krajina OG was located. So if a unit had captured an HVO member, the unit would transfer the prisoner to the OG command, and the OG command would then send that prisoner to the Zenica KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, when you say "these barracks in Travnik," that was the former JNA barracks in Travnik. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At any point in time while you were the OG Bosanska Krajina president of the exchange commission, did you go to the location at the former JNA barracks in Travnik where HVO soldiers were temporarily deprived of their freedom?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you, sir, about any knowledge that you might have about the units which constituted the OG Bosanska Krajina during the time period that you were affiliated with that operational group. Do you know what units of the 3rd Corps of the ABiH were part of the operations group Bosanska Krajina from April 1993 onwards? Until November 1993? Do you know which units?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: I couldn't say. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the approximate area of responsibility of the operations group Bosanska Krajina during the time period from April 1993 through November 1993?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: No, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the time period that you were affiliated with the OG Bosanska Krajina commission on exchange, were you aware of any subordinate units of the OG Bosanska Krajina keeping surrendered HVO soldiers in any location other than the former JNA barracks in Travnik, which you've already told us about?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of any such cases.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, let me ask you a few questions -- before I do that, do you recall -- you told us earlier about the time that you were in -- June of 1993 in Guca Gora at the monastery with Mr. Eminovic and Mr. Beba?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you be more specific in terms of the date in June 1993 when you were there?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: I can't remember the date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, the date that the ABiH took control of Guca Gora?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: I don't know that date either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But it was certainly after that date that you were in Guca Gora with Mr. Beba and Mr. Eminovic. Is that correct? It was after the ABiH had taken control of Guca Gora?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: Well, as I said, we found members of the military police of the 306th Brigade, they were providing security for the monastery. And since that was the case, the army had already taken control of that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately how many members of the 306th Mountain Brigade military police were at the monastery in Guca Gora on the day you visited in June 1993?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: All I can say is how many of them there were at the entrance. As I said, there were PATs and PAMs firing on that entire area on the road, so I entered the monastery rapidly. So perhaps there were three or four policemen who were standing in front of the gate to the monastery.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm a bit confused. I'm hoping you can help me here. Are you telling us that at the time you, Mr. Beba, and Mr. Eminovic arrived, that there was still combat going on? Because you say "firing on that area on the road, so I entered the monastery rapidly."

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: I don't know how I could explain what was happening in the area. But that part of the road that I'm talking about, it was always dangerous, throughout the conflict that we had with the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So at the time period the three of you arrived and entered the monastery, there was incoming -- I believe you said PAM or PAT fire at the time you entered the monastery?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether there was firing at the time. But that part of the road was always dangerous. And later on, when I worked in Zenica, when I would travel to Zenica, I would always turn the lights off when driving. That part of the road was always dangerous. There was sporadic firing opened at the vehicles using that road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I believe you told us earlier, page 28, line 15, that Mr. Beba spoke to a priest and others who were standing by the monastery. Was that conversation inside the monastery or outside the monastery?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: Inside the monastery.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you happen to recall or do you know the name or names of any of those people that Mr. Beba spoke with, including the priest?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: I don't know the names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to ask you a few questions, if I may, about the exchange involving Ensud Kadiric. You were involved in the exchange of Mr. Kadiric. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell us what you recall about that situation. Can you tell us the specifics about how you became involved and what that exchange was all about.

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: I was involved in this exchange at the time when I was already the president of the commission for POWs in the 3rd Corps. And I remember that this person was someone who had been wounded, and the International Red Cross insisted on having this soldier released. They were the most insistent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I would also like to know if General Alagic was personally pressuring you to get this individual released? Was that the case?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: General Alagic always exerted such pressure. He wanted all army members who had been imprisoned to be released as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you know if General Alagic was related in any way to Ensud Kadiric?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall the approximate date of the exchange involving Mr. Kadiric? The time period?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: I think it was at the beginning of 1994.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did that exchange take place?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: I'm trying to remember. But since there were a number of such exchanges, I can't remember whether it took place in the direction of Travnik or in the direction of Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just ask you, I neglected to ask you earlier, sir. When we were talking about individuals or captured HVO soldiers in the vicinity of Travnik, do you happen to know or do you have any recollection of any captured HVO soldiers being detained in the area around Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "no," sir, is it no, there weren't any detained, or no, you have no recollection of anyone being detained there?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with any such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, with the assistance of the usher, I would ask the witness be shown Prosecution Exhibit P655, please. I believe we do have additional copies if that would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'd ask you to take a look at the document. It might be easier, sir, on the projector which is to your right. You'll see the document. Let me ask you, please, if you could just take a moment and look at this document and let us know whether this is a document that you have ever seen before.

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: Yes, I've already seen this document. This is one of my reports on negotiations with the HVO exchange commission.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be correct, then, sir, that you were actually the author of this document?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please look approximately the middle of the page under number 12, and I note that there are two groupings or two clusters of numbers 1 through 12. The first one, I'm talking about the first one, the first time the number 12 appears. Can you tell us what that indicates.

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: Well, I'm informing the commander of the identity of the POWs whom the Croatian side wants released. And I'm informing them of the army members that the HVO commission is offering. Under number 12, the HVO commission informs me that they weren't even aware of the name because they had information according to which there was some kind of a prison in Mehurici. That's why the name isn't mentioned here. All it says is that there is a prisoner that they have, according to information that the HVO commission has.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall whether or not you took any steps to attempt to identify this otherwise unidentified Croat prisoner in Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: How should I explain this? We tried to check if there were any prisoners of war in Mehurici. And whether there's something that was not in accordance with the commander's order, for all the prisoners to be transferred immediately to the prison in Zenica. We learned that there were no prisoners up there. I would like to say one more thing in order to clarify the matter: Very often during those negotiations, for example, I would receive information that the HVO commission, in other words, the HVO kept some of our members prisoner in the cinema hall in Vitez and elsewhere. I would forward this information to the HVO. However, very few or almost no such cases were ever resolved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you a couple of follow-on questions to what you've just told us, sir. You said, "We tried to check whether there were any prisoners of war in Mehurici," and then the second sentence after that says: "We learned that there were no prisoners up there." When you said, "We learned that there were no prisoners up there," were you referring to Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: No. I was saying that save for the prisoners who were recorded in the prison in Zenica, there were no other prisoners held by the ABiH.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, when you say: "We tried to check if there were any prisoners of war in Mehurici," do you recall approximately when that was that you made this attempt to see if there were prisoners in Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR SEFER
utterances.text: After the negotiations, a query was sent to all the brigades in order to check whether they had any prisoners of war from the ranks of the HVO.
